extracted.intended_audience: aspiring and local stand-up comedians, indie show producers and promoters (alt/scene-building)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance for producing, promoting, and curating alt/independent stand-up comedy shows and building a local comedy scene. Covers venue selection, lineups, promotion, community norms, and expectations for performers and producers.

rubrics_metrics.name: Only promote things worth promoting
rubrics_metrics.description: Only promote things worth promoting.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Your word is on the line; if you send people to shitty open mics, overpriced venues or blah events they will never trust your recommendation again and think less of standup. Don’t promote low-quality shows just to push names out.

rubrics_metrics.name: Put comedy ahead of your ego
rubrics_metrics.description: Put comedy ahead of your ego.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Refuse complacency and pandering for cheap laughs. Don’t act superior, treat comics as tools for personal gain, or expect things because of status. Accept that you are owed nothing; do the work, improve craft, avoid entitlement that kills art.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue and atmosphere is everything
rubrics_metrics.description: Venue and atmosphere is everything.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The venue is often the single biggest difference between success and failure. An okay set in the right venue can be great; a great set in the wrong venue can fail. Think room dynamics, intimacy, staging, sound, seating, temperature, location and front-of-house practices.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intimate room
rubrics_metrics.description: Intimate room: Find something that can seat 50 people comfortably, 80 packed to capacity, but still feel good if 15 show up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Room dynamics affect show quality and future turnout. Put small tables up front to encourage audience proximity; avoid lining the back with round tables; sit in every chair to check sightlines; an empty front row makes the event feel blah even if full.

rubrics_metrics.name: Separate from the bar
rubrics_metrics.description: Separate from the bar: if you can get a dedicated show room for comedy, jump on it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Dedicated rooms force the audience to be people there for the show and limit distractions from walk-ins, darts, and loud bar equipment (e.g., margarita machines killing punchlines). Bar shows create noise and wandering audiences that hurt comedy.

rubrics_metrics.name: Staging should be sparse, tasteful, cheap
rubrics_metrics.description: Staging: sparse, tasteful, cheap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Stage should provide elevation without uncomfortable viewing; soft LED top light works. Keep it dark and intimate. Avoid comics stepping out of the light and relying on crowd work. Avoid long shotgun-style stages; arrange seating half-circle when possible. Little candles help mood.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sound: reliable mic and PA with proper EQ
rubrics_metrics.description: Holy shit do people ignore this. Yes – you need a mic and a PA.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use a proper PA, set treble up, scoop mids a bit, raise bass appropriately. Walk the room during performance to check audibility; laughter affects sound. Ensure speaker placement doesn’t make front cringe while back strains to hear.

rubrics_metrics.name: Seating configuration
rubrics_metrics.description: Seats: up close. Tables up front. Single chairs in the middle – high tops around the back edges.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seating arrangement affects intimacy and connection. Prioritize audience proximity to the stage to improve engagement and perception of show fullness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Temperature control
rubrics_metrics.description: Temperature: avoid warm, avoid hot.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Slight chill keeps people alert, laughing, and drinking; it helps audience engagement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Location and parking
rubrics_metrics.description: Location and parking: find a place where people would want to go.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Good bar, designated smoking patio, safe parking, and convenient distance matter. Don’t pick a location just because it has foot traffic if the crowd will resent the show invading their space.

rubrics_metrics.name: House management during shows (front-of-house practices)
rubrics_metrics.description: During shows: Don’t open doors until ~15 minutes before show; have someone seat people; play upbeat music before/after; lower lights when show starts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Keep pre/post-show music so silence isn’t creepy. Have volunteers run door/music. Police the room for hecklers: politely and immediately remove disruptive patrons to train audience behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Approaching venues
rubrics_metrics.description: Approaching Venues: Choose the best night, talk to management, make no promises of immediate crowds, and be willing to spend a year developing the night.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t accept shitty nights (e.g., nights with major competing events). Don’t expect venue support; take responsibility for promotion. If you prove the show you may negotiate small cash, but build the show first and then get the venue behind it. Get guarantees for time/space to avoid hassles.

rubrics_metrics.name: Know your audience; have good taste
rubrics_metrics.description: Know Your audience. Have Good Taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize that many attendees put comedy second to drinking/socializing. Decide the show's goal and curate accordingly. Avoid booking cheap pandering or repetitive offensive tropes; develop taste so the audience and performers can grow. The jokes still must be funny and well-performed.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid ethnic-themed or pandering shows without purpose
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid ethnic themed shows for most cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These can attract crowds but often trap performers into stereotype-based material and prevent artistic growth. If you do a themed show, be intentional; don’t default to lazy racial joke lineups.

rubrics_metrics.name: You can’t do it alone / build a working group
rubrics_metrics.description: You Can’t Do It Alone.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Sustaining a show requires a group of comics who will share responsibilities: promo, door, music, booking. Assign simple duties so performers can still do their writing and stage work. One person can do it once or twice, but long-term requires collaboration.

rubrics_metrics.name: Lineups: create a show identity and curate acts
rubrics_metrics.description: Lineups: present comics you love to watch; create a named monthly show showcasing quality acts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Build substance rather than promoting your name. A show about good comedy earns trust. Don’t fill posters with unknown names; promote the show’s quality and trust will grow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Host must be a good comic
rubrics_metrics.description: Your host has to be a good comic who can keep a show together.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Don’t put a rookie or someone who won’t do the hosting work just because they bring a crowd. Hosting is hard, dedicated work—pick someone who can control tone and transitions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Start on time and lead off with your best comics
rubrics_metrics.description: Start on time and lead off with the best comics you have.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Starting late or saving the good acts for later trains audiences to arrive late and treat the show as filler. Structure the lineup to build engagement early.

rubrics_metrics.name: Mix acts for variety and allow risk-taking
rubrics_metrics.description: Mix up the acts for variety; toward the end, include performers taking chances.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Blend polished performers with those experimenting. Give freedom to fail—especially mid- or later-show spots—to foster growth and future payoff.

rubrics_metrics.name: Everybody performing promotes
rubrics_metrics.description: Everybody performing promotes: make it a must.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a performer refuses to promote their own appearance, don’t book them. Performers unwilling to bring audiences signal they aren’t invested and will hurt the show.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid poison: remove toxic contributors
rubrics_metrics.description: Avoid Poison: don’t surround yourself with negative, toxic comics.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Toxic people kill momentum—negativity, treating newbies poorly, and constant complaining destroys atmosphere. If someone undermines the scene, ask them to leave the organizing group.

rubrics_metrics.name: Encourage community norms; push past faux social anxiety
rubrics_metrics.description: Social anxiety commentary: hang after shows, thank people, be a person.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Most people aren’t genuinely debilitated by anxiety—encourage comics to support each other, network, and engage audiences rather than hide or act entitled. Reinforce supportive audience behavior by example.

rubrics_metrics.name: Creativity over cheap funny/pandering
rubrics_metrics.description: Creativity over Funny: being creative should trump pandering for laughs.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage ideas that push material forward. Being merely funny via cheap pandering limits growth; creativity generates momentum and sustained improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Promotion must be multi-channel, repeated, and consistent
rubrics_metrics.description: Actually promote. Then do it again. And Again…
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No single promotion tool works reliably. Use multiple tools in combination, start early, and repeat. Booking acts people want helps but constant, consistent promotion across channels is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show naming and branding
rubrics_metrics.description: Start with the name of your show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A clear, appealing show name helps marketing. Promote the show identity rather than individual unknown names on the lineup.

rubrics_metrics.name: Facebook event strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Facebook: Create an event and a meme you can tag performers in.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage shares and likes; don’t rely solely on Facebook (algorithms favor engaged posts). If you have a show page, insist performers invite relevant friends; avoid inviting irrelevant/out-of-town people who won’t attend.

rubrics_metrics.name: Text and instant-messaging etiquette
rubrics_metrics.description: Text and Instant Messaging: Be polite, be sincere, don’t be ‘Promoter Person’.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Respect friends’ boundaries; don’t hound people. Be genuine and personal—ask about them and show you care rather than treating them like cattle.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alt-weekly / press outreach
rubrics_metrics.description: Alt Weekly: most cities have them; reach out to the announcement editor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Message politely, invite them, stay in touch, and be patient. Buy them a drink; they’re busy and underpaid. Develop a relationship rather than expecting instant coverage.

rubrics_metrics.name: Flyer strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Flyers: make a small number and design them well.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Create professional-looking or intentionally cheesy flyers; don’t list a bunch of unknown names. Hand them out in person in places where you can engage people; don’t lazily stash them on cars or leave them in random places.

rubrics_metrics.name: Meetup and community group use
rubrics_metrics.description: Use Meetup groups: join or start one for your show.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Meetup can be a good tool to organize interested audiences and build a community pool for events.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instagram and Twitter use
rubrics_metrics.description: Instagram and Twitter: good to have, but depend on active promotion.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use social media to post photos of attended shows to demonstrate a crowd and build community, but platforms need a dedicated pool working them together to be effective.

rubrics_metrics.name: Collect contact info and follow up (most effective tactic)
rubrics_metrics.description: Talk to people, get emails, Facebooks, whatever. Follow up.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Collecting contact info and following up is the number one effective promotion tactic many avoid. Do the follow-up consistently, it works better than relying on passive social posts.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine promotion tools regularly
rubrics_metrics.description: All promotion tools must be used together and repeatedly.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: None will work alone 100% of the time. Use Facebook, texts, flyers, press, meetups, social media and follow-ups together on an ongoing basis.

rubrics_metrics.name: Big vs. small market strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Big vs. Small Market: tailor show frequency and expectations to market size.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Big markets have more talent but more competing open mics; small markets have eager comics but less ability to sustain frequent shows. Adjust show cadence (weekly vs monthly) to available talent and audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use mics to test material and reserve polished bits for promoted shows
rubrics_metrics.description: Jokes repeated bore and wear out an audience; constant new jokes that aren’t ready do the same.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Hit shitty mics to test and develop material; save a show worth promoting for mostly formed material so you look good to your building audience.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid entitlement and complacency
rubrics_metrics.description: Entitlement breeds complacency. Complacency kills art.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Encourage continual work and scene support; don’t let success cause performers to stop participating or promoting the scene that helped them.

rubrics_metrics.name: Monetization expectations: there is no money early
rubrics_metrics.description: There Is No Money.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Expect little to no monetary return early on. Use free/$5 shows, donations, or pay-what-you-want to cover costs. Beware promoters who exploit 'exposure' while taking cover charges—don’t be that promoter.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor grassroots shows once you move up
rubrics_metrics.description: If you succeed, honor the early shows that helped you.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Support and recognize grassroots/scene-building shows when you have national opportunities; don’t abandon or denigrate the scene that helped you grow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do the work right and follow through on your word
rubrics_metrics.description: Do the work right. Avoid paying lip service. Follow through on your word.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Credibility matters: fulfill promises to venues, performers, and audiences. Consistent delivery is essential for long-term scene-building.
